name: Caroli disease
aliases: communicating cavernous ectasia of the bile ducts

reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / AASLD
clinicalPearls: Characterised by congenital, non-obstructive saccular or fusiform dilatation of the large intrahepatic bile ducts
The term Caroli disease is used for isolated duct ectasia, whereas Caroli syndrome denotes the same duct changes combined with congenital hepatic fibrosis
Recurrent bacterial cholangitis, intrahepatic stone formation, and biliary sepsis are the dominant clinical problems
Cross-sectional imaging shows dilated ducts surrounding a portal vein branch, the so-called central dot sign, which is a helpful diagnostic clue
It is frequently linked with fibrocystic disease elsewhere, particularly autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease and medullary sponge kidney
Disease may be localised to one lobe or segment, in which case surgical resection can be curative, or diffuse and bilobar, which limits options
There is a meaningfully increased lifetime risk of cholangiocarcinoma, warranting long-term surveillance

Endoscopic and radiological drainage, stone clearance, and antibiotic treatment of cholangitis are mainstays, with transplantation considered for diffuse disease or with associated portal hypertension
reference.pathophysiology: Caroli disease is a ductal plate malformation, an inherited abnormality in the embryological remodelling of the biliary tree, and is often associated with mutations affecting ciliary proteins (notably PKHD1, shared with autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease). Arrest of duct plate development leaves the larger intrahepatic ducts abnormally and permanently dilated while remaining in communication with the biliary system. Bile stasis within these ectatic segments promotes intraductal stone formation and recurrent ascending bacterial infection. When the malformation also involves the smallest ducts, portal fibrosis develops (congenital hepatic fibrosis), producing Caroli syndrome with portal hypertension. Chronic inflammation and stasis underlie the elevated risk of malignant transformation to cholangiocarcinoma.
additionalDifferentials: Obstructive biliary dilatation from stones or stricture
additionalInvestigations: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography to map ductal anatomy and identify the central dot sign
Ultrasound and CT to detect stones, abscesses, and lobar distribution
Renal imaging to look for associated fibrocystic kidney disease
Blood cultures and inflammatory markers during suspected cholangitis
Tumour markers and targeted imaging where malignancy is suspected
Liver biopsy when congenital hepatic fibrosis or portal hypertension is in question
redFlags: Acute suppurative cholangitis with sepsis requiring urgent biliary drainage
Progressive jaundice or a dominant stricture raising concern for cholangiocarcinoma
Variceal bleeding or other decompensation when portal hypertension is present
reference.prognosis: Localised disease amenable to resection has a favourable outlook, whereas diffuse disease carries recurrent cholangitis, progressive biliary damage, and a significant long-term risk of cholangiocarcinoma; associated portal hypertension and renal disease also influence outcome.
pitfalls: Mistaking the ectatic ducts for obstructive dilatation and attempting inappropriate decompression
Failing to screen for associated renal fibrocystic disease
Underestimating the ongoing cholangiocarcinoma risk and omitting surveillance
Not distinguishing localised from diffuse disease before planning surgery
